try hard not think about the trauma

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: 'Avoid Exercise' is not clinically coherent with the rest of the profile. The threat items center on hypervigilance about nighttime intrusion and safety checking in the home, while the memory and appraisal items focus on intrusive assault memories, danger, and physical vulnerability. Exercise avoidance addresses a different symptom domain and lacks plausible linkage to the selected threat, memory, or appraisal content. In contrast, magical thinking and mirror checking fit better with maladaptive attempts to manage threat and distress.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: These two selected items are difficult to reconcile within the same profile. A strong appraisal of permanent bodily damage implies acknowledgment of serious ongoing physical consequences, whereas telling oneself the event did not really happen or was not that bad reflects minimization/denial of the trauma's reality or impact. While some ambivalence can occur clinically, this pair pulls in opposing directions strongly enough to question internal coherence in this profile.

vignette: Clara sat at her pottery wheel in the back room of her home, the damp clay cool against her palms, when the side door splintered inward. She had not heard the approach, only the sudden crack of wood and the heavy tread on the linoleum. A stranger stood in the doorway, breathing hard, demanding she hand over her savings. When she hesitated, the man shoved her backward, his knee driving into her sternum as he rifled through her cupboards. The struggle was brief but brutal, ending only when he fled into the night, leaving her curled on the concrete floor, gasping, the scent of spilled turpentine and fear thick in the air. Now widowed and alone, Clara had come to believe the world was no longer a place where she could simply live, and the studio that had held her work for forty years now felt like a trap. Over the following weeks, the memory would force its way into her mind the moment she closed her eyes. It was not a story she could follow, but a series of sharp, unblinking pictures: the splintered door, the man’s knuckles white around her wrist, the shadow stretching across her kiln. When those images surfaced, she felt as though the concrete floor were pressing against her back again, as though the assault were happening right now. She tried hard not to think about what happened. If she let her mind wander toward that night, she would not be able to handle it. Her body refused to rest. Even when she sat in her armchair with the windows locked and the lights on, she was unable to relax, her shoulders permanently tense, her pulse hammering. She had started waking during the night, drawn from sleep by a sudden, sharp awareness that she needed to verify her safety. She would sit up, listening for the faint scrape of a branch or the creak of settling timber, convinced that any sound might mean someone was entering her home again. The checking occupied her hours. She moved through the house at dawn and dusk, her fingers tracing the deadbolts, the latch on the studio door, the window frames, counting the clicks until she was certain every lock held. She kept a small hand mirror on the kitchen counter, finding herself catching her own reflection and immediately scanning her face, her hands, checking for marks or damage, as though looking away for a second might let the threat slip back in. The consequences of these habits accumulated quietly. She stopped opening the studio to her regular students, telling herself the door was too difficult to secure, and her commissions piled up in boxes she could no longer bear to touch. Her granddaughter stopped visiting after Clara insisted on locking the gate three times during dinner, the girl’s quiet sighs speaking louder than any argument. Clara knew she was making herself tired, knowing the world was dangerous, yet she felt her body kept reacting as if she were still in danger even when she was safe. It was the morning she dropped her teacup because the kettle’s hiss sounded too much like the crack of the splintered door that finally broke her patience. She had come to believe she could not carry the weight of her own vigilance anymore. Now, she sits in a quiet waiting room across town, her hands resting on her lap, hoping that someone might help her untangle the fear from her days. What frightens her most is not the memory itself, but the certainty that her body will never stop sounding the alarm, and that one day, she will simply run out of time to check the locks.
